meaning: A yellow background is traditionally read as consciousness, optimism and the light of the divine. It suggests a card that is clear, energetic and outward-looking.
A clear blue sky speaks of calm, spirit, intuition and peace of mind. Situations shown under it are usually open and untroubled, whatever the figures are doing.
Grey is often read as sorrow, uncertainty, neutrality or conflict held in suspension. It drains the scene of warmth and asks you to notice what is unresolved.
A black sky signals night, despair, the unknown or a moment of crisis. It is the darkest backdrop in the deck and marks a card's emotional low point or deepest mystery.

Clouds are the boundary between heaven and earth: they show spiritual forces at work, hidden factors, or thought that has not yet taken solid form. Gifts offered from a cloud come from a higher or unseen source.
Rain falling from heavy clouds is read as grief, release and tears. In the Three of Swords it shows sorrow pouring out, which is also the first step toward healing.
A lightning bolt is sudden revelation or shock: truth arriving all at once and breaking down what was built on false ground. It is divine fire striking from above.
A rainbow is a promise of harmony after hardship, a bridge between heaven and earth. On the Ten of Cups it is made of cups, crowning lasting emotional fulfilment.

Mountains far away usually stand for aspirations, ideals or abstract thought: goals still on the horizon, or challenges that lie ahead rather than right now. Snow-capped peaks often suggest spiritual heights.
Mountains close behind a figure, especially bare and rocky ones, show challenges already faced, hard-won authority or austerity. They can also mark the heights a figure has climbed to.
Rolling green hills suggest gentle progress, fertility and a settled, pleasant life. Standing on a hilltop can also show a vantage point or a position to defend.
Flat, open land suggests freedom of movement, plain dealing and things moving without obstacle. Ploughed fields add the idea of patient preparation and work that will bear fruit.
Sandy desert with pyramids, unique to the Wands court, suggests adventure, distant travel and the heat of the element of Fire. It can also hint at testing, dry conditions that only passion can cross.
Cultivated gardens, vines and flowering arches show abundance that has been tended over time, comfort, beauty and a safe, sheltered place. They are typical of Pentacles and of the Empress.
Running water is the flow of feeling and life over time. A river can carry you onward, separate two places, or mark a crossing from one stage of life to another.

The sea is the vast, deep unconscious and the full range of emotion. Calm water suggests peace and receptivity; choppy waves show emotional movement or unsettled times, and ships on it point to ventures and trade.
A still pool is the inner world, reflection and the source of intuition and dreams. Figures touching or standing in a pool are connecting the conscious mind with the subconscious.
A waterfall in the Empress's woodland shows emotion and life-force flowing freely, nourishing everything around it. It is abundance in motion.
Boats show emotional or literal journeys and the crossing from one state to another. Ships on the horizon are often read as plans, commerce and waiting for one's ventures to arrive.
Red is passion, desire, vitality, action and worldly power. Red robes and cloaks usually mark a figure who acts, rules or is driven by strong feeling.
White is purity, innocence, truth and spiritual clarity. White robes or a white horse suggest motives that are clean or a force beyond the personal.
Blue is calm, intuition, the subconscious and the element of Water. Blue clothing often marks a reflective, receptive or emotionally attuned figure.
Green is growth, nature, fertility, hope and renewal. It is common on figures who are youthful, hopeful or close to the earth.
Purple is traditionally linked to spiritual authority, wisdom and dignity. It is often worn by figures who mediate between higher and lower worlds.
Black stands for the unknown, endings, mourning and what is hidden. It can be frightening, as in Death or the Devil, or simply mark a necessary passage through darkness.
Gold and bright yellow suggest the sun, intellect, achievement and divine light. Golden cups and coins point to things of real and lasting value.

Unclothed figures traditionally show innocence, honesty and nothing hidden: the soul in its natural state. Context matters, as nakedness can also suggest vulnerability, as with the chained pair on the Devil.
A blindfold shows deliberately not looking: a decision being avoided, a mind turned inward, or a sense of being trapped by one's own perception. It also asks you to trust inner sight.
Kneeling shows humility, devotion, petition or receptivity. It can mean surrender to something larger, or asking for help.
When we see a figure from behind we share their view and are invited into their situation. It often shows looking ahead to the future, leaving something behind, or a private, inward moment.
In much modern reading practice, facing left is linked with the past, receptivity and the inner world. A figure riding or walking leftward may be returning, reflecting or retreating.
Facing right is often linked with the future, action and the outer world. Riders heading right are usually read as advancing toward something.
A seated figure looking straight out is stable, authoritative and fully present. These cards often feel like the figure is addressing you directly.
A raised hand or arm channels power, gives blessing or proclaims. The Magician's one-hand-up, one-hand-down gesture means 'as above, so below'.
A bowed head or hidden face shows grief, regret, burden or exhaustion. Notice what the figure is not looking at, which is often the hope still left in the card.
Angels are messengers of higher guidance, blessing and integration. They appear at key turning points of the Major Arcana.
Every Ace shows a hand emerging from a cloud, offering the suit's gift. It signals a fresh opportunity that seems to come from beyond yourself: it is offered, and you choose whether to take it.

A crown is authority, mastery and responsibility over a domain. Its decoration tells you what kind of rule: stars for heavenly power, plain gold for worldly power, flowers or wings for gentler or airier rule.
Laurel and olive wreaths are classical symbols of victory, honour and recognition. On the World the great wreath frames a cycle completed.
Garlands and flower crowns show celebration, joy, fertility and harmony with nature.
Armour shows protection, readiness for action, discipline and sometimes defensiveness. It marks a figure prepared to fight or to hold firm.
The lion is strength, courage, pride and the element of Fire, as well as the sign Leo. A tamed or gentle lion shows passion mastered by inner strength rather than force.
Dogs are loyalty, companionship and the tamed side of our instincts. The Fool's little dog can be a warning or an encouraging friend.
On the Moon the wolf howls beside the dog: the wild, untamed instinct set against the domesticated one. Together they show the push and pull of the subconscious.
Horses carry the energy of movement, drive and progress. How the horse moves (charging, plodding, prancing) mirrors the pace of the situation, and a white horse adds purity or triumph.
Birds are messengers, thought and the element of Air, bridging earth and sky. A dove brings peace and spirit; a hooded falcon shows desire disciplined and kept under control.
Fish rise from the waters of the unconscious: surprise insights, creativity and emotional messages. The fish in the Page of Cups' cup is an unexpected feeling or idea surfacing.
Butterflies are transformation and the soul, and belong to the element of Air. They decorate the thrones of the Queen and King of Swords.
The man (or angel), eagle, lion and bull in the corners stand for the four fixed signs (Aquarius, Scorpio, Leo, Taurus) and the four elements. They show the whole cosmos in balance.
The serpent is wisdom, temptation, renewal and the rising life-force. It can be a healing caduceus or the tempter in the tree, so read it with its context.
Sphinxes guard mysteries and pose riddles. On the Chariot one black and one white sphinx show opposing forces that must be steered together.
Red roses stand for passion, desire and love in its active, worldly form. In the Magician's garden they pair with white lilies to show desire balanced with purity.
The white rose is purity, innocence and freedom from base desire. The Fool carries one; on Death's banner it promises renewal after the ending.
White lilies mean purity of thought and spiritual intention; irises on Temperance are linked with Iris, the rainbow messenger. Water lilies on the Ace of Cups show emotion opening like a flower.
Sunflowers turn toward the light: joy, vitality, loyalty and success. They are a sign of warmth and optimism.
Grapes and vines show abundance, pleasure, fertility and the rewards of cultivation. With the Devil they can also hint at overindulgence.
Ripening wheat is fertility, harvest and nourishment: what was planted coming to fruition.
The pomegranate is feminine fertility, hidden knowledge and the mysteries of the Underworld (Persephone's fruit). It decorates the High Priestess's veil and the Empress's gown.
Trees show growth, stability and the connection between earth and heaven. Wind-bent trees show strain; the two trees of the Lovers are the Tree of Life and the Tree of Knowledge.

The horizontal figure eight means infinity, eternal life and endless flow of energy. Above a head it shows mastery that is spiritual rather than forced; around coins it shows the endless juggling of life.
The crossed keys at the Hierophant's feet unlock spiritual knowledge and tradition, echoing the keys of heaven and earth given to St Peter.
Scales are justice, fairness, balance and karma: weighing things up and receiving exactly what is due. In the Six of Pentacles they also show measured generosity.
The sword is the element of Air: intellect, truth, decision and conflict. It can cut through confusion or wound, so look at who holds it and how.
The cup is the element of Water: love, emotion, relationships and intuition. An upright, filled cup receives and holds feeling.
The wand is the element of Fire: will, passion, creativity and ambition. Staffs and batons in the Major Arcana carry the same sense of directed energy.
The pentacle, a five-pointed star in a coin, is the element of Earth: money, body, work, home and the material world. On the Devil the inverted pentagram suggests spirit placed beneath matter.
The Hermit's lantern holds a six-pointed star: inner wisdom lighting the way just one step ahead.
A banner proclaims a message or a victory. Death's banner carries a white rose of renewal, the Sun's banner joyful energy, and Judgement's a red cross of resurrection.
The Emperor's sceptre is topped with an ankh, the Egyptian sign of life. It shows his authority as life-giving and lasting.
The cross unites spirit and matter, the vertical and horizontal. It marks sacred authority, balance of the elements, sacrifice and resurrection.
A turning wheel is cycles, fate, karma and change. What goes up comes down, and the centre stays still.

Paired pillars come from Solomon's Temple: Boaz (B, black) is strength and receptivity, Jachin (J, white) is establishment and activity. A figure seated between them holds the balance between opposites and guards a threshold.
Two towers form a gateway to the unknown. On the Moon and Death the path leads between them toward something beyond ordinary experience.

A throne is stability, authority and a settled position. The carvings tell you the ruler's element: lions and salamanders for Fire, sea creatures for Water, butterflies for Air, bulls and goats for Earth.
Castles stand for security, achievement and home, or for ambition built high. The struck Tower is a structure built on false foundations being torn down.
A bridge is a way across, a link to what lies on the other side. In the Five of Cups it shows that a path home still exists beyond the grief.
A wall marks a boundary: protection and security, but also limits. Standing on a parapet, the Two of Wands looks beyond the safe world he controls.

On the numbered Minor Arcana the count of wands, cups, swords or pentacles is the card's number, and each number carries its own theme (one = beginnings, five = conflict, ten = completion). Count the objects and you already know half the meaning.
Each Major Arcana card carries a Roman numeral that places it on the Fool's journey from 0 to XXI. Numbers that share a digit sum (like V and XIV) are often read together.

The High Priestess's scroll reads TORA (the Law), and the letters around the Wheel spell TARO/ROTA (the wheel turns) along with the Hebrew letters of the divine name. They tie the deck to sacred law and cycles of fate.
The Hebrew letters Yod-He-Vau-He on the Wheel of Fortune spell the divine name. Small yods (Hebrew letter-shaped flames or drops) also fall on several cards as divine grace descending.
The ♀ symbol on the Empress's heart shield and on the Nine of Pentacles' gown links them to Venus: love, beauty, comfort and fertility.
The Moon rules intuition, dreams, cycles and the subconscious, as well as illusion. A crescent at a figure's feet or on the shoulders shows command of, or connection to, these hidden tides.
The Sun is life, clarity, joy, success and conscious awareness. A sun rising or setting on the horizon shows a dawn or ending of a cycle.
Stars are hope, guidance and the influence of the heavens. A crown or canopy of stars marks a figure under celestial protection.
Light around the head shows illumination, enlightenment or a higher state of awareness reached through the experience shown.
Small falling Hebrew yods, as flames or drops, are grace and divine energy descending into the world. Their meaning shifts with the card: blessing on the Aces, upheaval on the Tower.
